column3: The grand stone front of a Jesuit church that burned down in 1835, carved with saints, dragons and a Chinese inscription. It is the symbol of Macau and part of a UNESCO site.
A plaza with a wave-patterned pavement and pastel colonial buildings, at the heart of the historic center of Macau.
A temple for Mazu, the sea goddess, which the Portuguese heard locals call A-Ma-Gao, giving Macau its name. Incense coils hang over its courtyard.
A museum inside the old fortress, which tells the story of Macau from fishing village to a meeting place of China and Europe.
A hilltop fortress built by the Portuguese in the 17th century, with cannons and a view over the old city.
The Leal Senado is a Portuguese-style civic building with blue-and-white tiles and a courtyard, in the central square.
A yellow Baroque church with a white trim and green shutters, dating from the 16th century, one of the oldest in Macau.
A temple where, in 1844, China and the United States signed the first treaty between the two countries.
A 338-meter tower, with a glass-floored viewing deck, a skywalk around the outside and the world's highest commercial bungee jump.
A hill with a small chapel and a pousada, with a quiet view over the harbor and the old city.
The home of the writer and thinker Zheng Guanying, a big complex of Chinese and Western styles beside the old city.
A grand 19th-century merchant's mansion in the Chinese style with Western details, inside the historic center.
A flaky pastry shell with creamy custard and a caramelized top. The Macau version was developed from Portuguese pastéis de nata.
A juicy pork chop in a crisp bun, a simple, cheap and tasty Macau snack that locals love.
A crisp, crumbly cookie made with almonds or mung bean flour, sold in the shops along the old streets.
Thin slices of pork dried and grilled with sugar and soy, chewy and sweet, a famous Macau gift.
A warm milk pudding that sets when hot milk meets ginger juice, a simple dessert with a spicy kick.
A dessert of layers of whipped cream and crumbled biscuits that look like sawdust, hence the name.
Salted cod from Portugal soaked and cooked in a variety of ways, a staple of Macanese kitchens.
A Macanese chicken dish baked with coconut milk, potatoes and curry spices, which blends Portuguese and Asian flavors.
Grilled chicken in a spicy sauce of chili, garlic and peanut, a Macanese dish with a connection to Portugal's African colonies.
The Macanese are people of mixed Portuguese and Chinese ancestry, who developed their own language, food and customs.
Portuguese is an official language of Macau beside Chinese, so you can see it on street signs and tiles.
Gaming resorts are a major industry in Macau, and the city's casinos draw visitors from all over the world.
Every year on the 23rd of the third lunar month, devotees celebrate the sea goddess Mazu's birthday with parades and offerings.
A narrow lane in Taipa lined with shops and snack stalls, selling almond cookies, pork jerky and egg rolls.
Five green colonial houses beside a lake in Taipa, which now serve as a museum of Macanese life.
A small church in the old village of Taipa, with a white and yellow front and a quiet garden.
A giant resort modeled on Venice, with an indoor canal, gondolas and painted skies.
A hill in Taipa with walking paths and a tower, which gives wide views over the islands.
Crab cooked in a rich, creamy curry with coconut and spices, a favorite seafood dish.
A quiet village of pastel houses, small plazas, and old shops, which feels like old Macau.
A small yellow chapel in Coloane that honors St. Francis Xavier, with a peaceful plaza in front.
A beach of dark sand on Coloane, with a park and a long, calm shore.
A small temple for Tin Hau, the sea goddess, tucked beside the fishing village of Coloane.
The famous egg tart from Lord Stow's bakery in Coloane, created by the English baker Andrew Stow in 1989.
A village where dried fish are hung up in the sun and old boats rest by the shore, a reminder of Coloane's fishing past.
